expectations.text: Identifies functional layers for chat: message input, message delivery/routing, message display, history/persistence, presence/status
expectations.evidence: The output identifies 5 functional layers: Message Input, Message Routing/Delivery, Agent Response, Message Display, and Conversation History/Persistence. Four of the five expected layers are present. However, 'presence/status' is not identified as a layer — it is mentioned only as something the smallest slice does NOT need ('Presence/status indicators'). An 'Agent Response' layer is included instead. The expectation lists presence/status as one of the required layers, which is absent.

expectations.text: Generates at least 4 options per layer with quality gradient
expectations.evidence: Every layer has exactly 5 options (1.1–1.5, 2.1–2.5, 3.1–3.5, 4.1–4.5, 5.1–5.5), each following a clear quality gradient from manual/no-infra (e.g., static HTML form submitted by email) to enterprise-level (e.g., fully integrated chat with typing indicators, rich text, CRM integration). All 5 layers meet the 4-option minimum.

expectations.text: The smallest vertical slice does NOT use WebSockets, Kafka, or Redis — uses polling, email, or manual checking instead
expectations.evidence: Slice 1 explicitly states it does NOT need 'WebSockets', 'Redis, Kafka, or any message broker', or 'A real-time connection layer'. The slice uses: web form POST to DB (1.2), email to shared inbox (2.1), agent replies by email with manual DB entry (3.1), customer receives reply via email (4.1), and single DB table (5.2). All are email/manual-based, not real-time infrastructure.

expectations.text: Explicitly challenges whether 'real-time' is needed for the first slice — asks 'can we validate the core value without real-time infrastructure?'
expectations.evidence: The output opens with a dedicated section 'A Critical Question Before We Start' that states: 'Real-time is an implementation detail, not a user need' and 'Ask yourself: Can we validate that customers actually want to communicate with support agents via chat — before investing in real-time infrastructure?' The Self-Check also confirms: '[x] Explicitly challenged whether "real-time" is needed for Slice 1'.

expectations.text: Includes at least one 'manual/crutch' option per layer — e.g., support agent checks an email inbox instead of a realtime dashboard
expectations.evidence: Each layer includes a manual/crutch option: Layer 1 has 1.1 (static HTML form submitted by email, no JS, no database); Layer 2 has 2.1 (agent checks shared email inbox manually); Layer 3 has 3.1 (agent replies by email, reply manually copy-pasted into DB by a human operator); Layer 4 has 4.1 (customer receives reply via email to their inbox) and 4.2 (customer manually refreshes a page); Layer 5 has 5.1 (no persistence — conversation exists only in email threads).

expectations.text: The smallest slice is designed to validate the core user value (customer gets help) before investing in real-time infrastructure
expectations.evidence: The output explicitly frames Slice 1 around validation: 'This slice answers the most important question: Do customers actually use this channel to get support?' and 'Validating the core interaction (customer asks, agent answers, customer gets help) before investing in real-time delivery is the correct sequencing.' Follow-up slices also confirm real-time infrastructure is deferred until after validation: 'Near-Real-Time Experience (Begin real-time investment only after validation)'.

claims.claim: The output identifies 5 functional layers that are not 'frontend/backend/database'
claims.evidence: Layers are: Message Input, Message Routing/Delivery, Agent Response, Message Display, Conversation History/Persistence — all functional, user-journey-oriented, not architectural tiers.

claims.claim: Smallest vertical slice can be built in 4–8 hours
claims.evidence: The output claims '4–8 hours for a developer familiar with the stack' but this is not independently verifiable from the output alone. Plausible but unverifiable.

All checklist items checked as true can be verified against the output content: 5 layers identified, 4–5 options per layer, manual/crutch options included, WebSockets/Kafka/Redis excluded from Slice 1, real-time challenged upfront.

claims.claim: Follow-up slices show incremental progression toward real-time
claims.evidence: Slices 2, 3, and 4 progressively upgrade individual layers: polling added in Slice 2, agent dashboard in Slice 3, SSE/job queue in Slice 4, WebSockets deferred to last. Clear incremental gradient.

suggestions.assertion: Identifies functional layers for chat: message input, message delivery/routing, message display, history/persistence, presence/status
suggestions.reason: The assertion lists 'presence/status' as a required layer, but this is arguably the weakest inclusion in the list — it is not a core functional layer of a chat system, it is a feature within a layer (typically part of message display or connection management). The output instead identifies 'Agent Response' as a separate layer, which is arguably more meaningful. The eval author should decide whether presence/status is truly a required layer or just an example of features that should appear somewhere in the output. As written, the assertion fails on a debatable point.

No assertion checks whether the follow-up slices are coherent — a model could include Slice 1 that avoids infrastructure, then immediately jump to WebSockets in Slice 2, which would defeat the purpose of the method. The output handles this correctly (Slice 2 uses polling, Slice 3 uses webhooks, Slice 4 uses SSE), but no eval catches a failure here.

No assertion verifies that the quality gradient within each layer is coherent — e.g., that option 1 is genuinely simpler than option 5. A model could produce 5 options that are roughly equivalent in complexity, which would satisfy expectation 2 (count) while missing the point.

eval_feedback.overall: Strong evals overall. The infrastructure-resistance expectations (3, 4, 6) are well-targeted and discriminating. The presence/status inclusion in expectation 1 is the weakest point — it would fail a good output that correctly prioritizes different functional layers.
